claim: Maintaining attention at a task-relevant spatial location while making eye-movements necessitates a rapid, saccade-synchronized shift of attentional modulation from the neuronal population representing the task-relevant location before the saccade to the one representing it after the saccade.
source: Maintaining attention at a task-relevant spatial location while making eye-movements necessitates a rapid, saccade-synchronized shift of attentional modulation from the neuronal population representing the task-relevant location before the saccade to the one representing it after the saccade.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about retinotopic visual processing and the need for attentional shifts across saccades.

claim: Spatial attention is fully available at the task-relevant location within 30 milliseconds after the saccade.
source: Using a fine-grained temporal analysis of human peri-saccadic detection performance in an attention task, we show that spatial attention is fully available at the task-relevant location within 30 milliseconds after the saccade.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from the study showing performance recovery within 30 ms post-saccade.

claim: Subjects tracked the attentional target veridically throughout the task, almost never responding to non-target stimuli.
source: Subjects tracked the attentional target veridically throughout our task: i.e. they almost never responded to non-target stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by the low false-positive rates observed in the experimental data.

claim: The processing of vision and visuospatial attention mostly proceeds via retinotopic representations in the brain.
source: The processing of vision and visuospatial attention mostly proceeds via retinotopic representations in the brain (Cavanagh et al., 2010; Wurtz, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Each saccadic eye-movement leads to a change in the retinotopic representation of the visual scene.
source: Since each saccadic eye-movement leads to a change in the retinotopic representation of the visual scene, maintaining attention at a task-relevant spatial location across a saccade necessitates a rapid, saccade-synchronized shift of attentional modulation from the neuronal population representing the task-relevant location before the saccade to the one representing it after the saccade (Marino and Mazer, 2016; Yao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about retinotopic processing and is also supported by citations.

claim: Previous perceptual measurements in humans suggest a neuronal attention shift that starts before the saccade and continues after the saccade ends.
source: Currently, perceptual measurements in humans suggest a neuronal attention shift that starts before the saccade and continues after the saccade ends (Rolfs et al., 2011; Szinte et al., 2015; Golomb et al., 2008, 2010a, 2011; Jonikaitis et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The precise time at which spatial attention becomes fully allocated to the task-relevant location after the saccade remains unclear based on previous measurements.
source: However, because these previous measurements used coarse temporal sampling and/or long-duration attentional probes, the precise time at which spatial attention becomes fully allocated to the task-relevant location after the saccade remains unclear.
evidence: This is an inference based on limitations of previous studies mentioned in the text.

claim: The rapid post-saccadic recovery of performance indicates that retinotopic attentional shifts occur within the time required to recover from saccadic suppression of vision.
source: This rapid post-saccadic recovery of performance in our attention task indicates that retinotopic attentional shifts occur within the time required to recover from saccadic suppression of vision.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing rapid recovery.

claim: Subjects responded to a distractor change on only 2.2% and 2% of trials in Experiments 1 and 2 respectively.
source: In both Experiments 1 and 2, overall, subjects responded to a distractor change on only 2.2% and 2% of trials respectively.
evidence: This is directly measured data from the experiments.

claim: At times well before and well after the saccade, subjects almost always detected the target change and their performance was near 100%.
source: At times well before and well after the saccade, subjects almost always detected the target change and their performance was near 100%.
evidence: This is supported by the performance data shown in the figures.

claim: Performance began to drop around the time the fixation point jumped.
source: Performance began to drop around the time the fixation point jumped (dashed vertical line in Figure 2A), as expected from the previously reported diversion of pre-saccadic attentional resources towards the saccade task (Deubel and Schneider, 1996; Montagnini and Castet, 2007; Hoffman and Subramaniam, 1995) and the post-saccadic retinotopic location (Szinte et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and by citations to previous research.

claim: Performance dropped steeply right before the saccade due to saccadic suppression.
source: The performance then dropped steeply right before the saccade, as expected from the drop in visual sensitivity due to saccadic suppression (Diamond et al., 2000; Dorr and Bex, 2013; McConkie and Loschky, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous research on saccadic suppression.

claim: Performance recovered back to baseline within 30 ms of saccade offset.
source: Importantly, our data show (for the first time in an attention task, to our knowledge) that performance recovered back to baseline within 30 ms of saccade offset (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The rapid time-course of recovery resembles that previously shown for saccadic suppression of visual performance in tasks without any requirement to maintain attention on a target across a saccade.
source: The rapid time-course of recovery resembles that previously shown for saccadic suppression of visual performance in tasks where visual sensitivity was probed around a saccade using a briefly flashed change, but without any requirement to maintain attention on a target across a saccade (Diamond et al., 2000; Dorr and Bex, 2013; McConkie and Loschky, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited previous research.

claim: The peri-saccadic attentional shift necessitated by retinotopic visual processing does not impose an additional temporal cost on the recovery from saccadic suppression.
source: This suggests that while resumption of visual function after a saccade is constrained by the recovery from saccadic suppression (Krekelberg, 2010), the peri-saccadic attentional shift necessitated by retinotopic visual processing does not impose an additional temporal cost on this recovery.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the similarity in recovery time-courses between the current study and previous studies on saccadic suppression.

claim: In a mental curve-tracing task with a fixed attentional target, attentional effects in monkey V1 emerge approximately 80 ms after the end of the saccade.
source: The rapid post-saccadic attentional availability at the target location that we infer from our data is consistent with the only physiological data on this issue: in a mental curve-tracing task similar to ours with a fixed attentional target, attentional effects in monkey V1 emerge approximately 80 ms after the end of the saccade (Khayat et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous physiological research.

claim: A change occurring 30 ms after saccade offset would reach the visual cortex at approximately the time when its neurons representing the target after the saccade are attentionally enhanced.
source: Given an onset latency of approximately 30 to 50 ms in monkey V1, MT and LIP (Khayat et al., 2004; Bair et al., 2002; Bisley et al., 2004), a change occurring 30 ms after saccade offset would reach the visual cortex at approximately the time when its neurons representing the target after the saccade are attentionally enhanced.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited onset latencies and the timing of attentional enhancement.

claim: By about 75 ms before the saccade, attentional enhancement could be seen at the 'post-saccadic' retinotopic location.
source: In fact, prior findings measuring discrimination performance for attentional probes at different locations suggest that by about 75 ms before the saccade, attentional enhancement could be seen at the 'post-saccadic' retinotopic location (which would be the wrong pre-saccadic spatial location) (Rolfs et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: After the saccade, attention stays at the pre-saccadic retinotopic location for up to 100 ms after the saccade according to other studies.
source: Other studies report that after the saccade, attention stays at the pre-saccadic retinotopic location (which would be the wrong post-saccadic spatial location) for up to 100 ms after the saccade (Golomb et al., 2008, 2010b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The predictive emergence of attention is consistent with single-neuron data from monkeys showing predictive responses in different attentional control areas of the brain.
source: The predictive emergence of attention is consistent with single-neuron data from monkeys showing predictive responses in different attentional control areas of the brain (Wurtz, 2008; Duhamel et al., 1992), while imaging data from humans have been presented as evidence for persistent retinotopic neural activity (Golomb et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous physiological research.

claim: In the time interval immediately after the saccade (0–150 ms), the data from both Experiments showed no statistically significant increase in the rate of false-positives due to retinotopic persistence.
source: In the time interval immediately after the saccade (0–150 ms), the data from both Experiments showed no statistically significant increase in the rate of false-positives due to retinotopic persistence (compared to the control location; all p-values>0.16, Boschloo's test; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Experiment 3 led to a false-positive rate of less than 1.4% and no evidence for an effect of either predictive shifts or retinotopic persistence on the false-positive rate.
source: An additional experiment (Experiment 3; Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary file 1B) where we changed the task design to test both pre-saccadic predictive shifts and post-saccadic retinotopic persistence (while making distractor changes more numerous and salient) also led to a false-positive rate of less than 1.4% and no evidence for an effect of either predictive shifts or retinotopic persistence on the false-positive rate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: The peri-saccadic spread of attention to irrelevant spatial locations reported in previous studies does not seem to have any manifest effects in our task.
source: Subjects thus tracked the attentional target veridically throughout our task, and the peri-saccadic spread of attention to irrelevant spatial locations reported in previous studies does not seem to have any manifest effects in our task.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low false-positive rates observed in the experiments.

claim: One important difference between our task and previous tasks was that we included only one attended location within each trial, and stimuli at all other locations were distractors that the subject had to ignore.
source: One important difference between our task and previous tasks was that we included only one attended location within each trial, and stimuli at all other locations were distractors that the subject had to ignore.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In previous tasks, all stimulus locations on each trial were potential targets and there were no distractor stimuli.
source: In contrast, the previous tasks required subjects to report a probe stimulus that could appear at any of the stimulus locations. There were no distractor stimuli, and attention was instead manipulated by using a dual-task (Rolfs et al., 2011; Golomb et al., 2008, 2010b) or using an exogenous cue (Jonikaitis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations describing previous experimental designs.

claim: Distractor filtering due to the attentional selection/weighting of sensory signals across the visual field is well-synchronized to the saccade and therefore does not spread to irrelevant spatial locations.
source: In this scenario, distractor filtering due to the attentional selection/weighting of sensory signals across the visual field is well-synchronized to the saccade and therefore does not spread to irrelevant spatial locations.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed results.

claim: Attentional signal enhancement, but not distractor filtering, is influenced by the predictive shifts and post-saccadic retinotopic persistence of attentional modulation in the brain.
source: In contrast, attentional signal enhancement, but not distractor filtering, is influenced by the predictive shifts and post-saccadic retinotopic persistence of attentional modulation in the brain.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for differences between the current and previous studies.

claim: The observed differences could be a result of task-dependent (or even entirely different) attentional mechanisms operating in the different tasks.
source: Even more generally, the observed differences could be a result of task-dependent (or even entirely different) attentional mechanisms operating in the different tasks.
evidence: This is speculation about alternative explanations.

claim: The data represent the first temporally fine-grained measurements of detection performance in an attention task in the critical immediate post-saccadic period (0 to 100 ms following saccade offset).
source: We provide the first temporally fine-grained measurements of detection performance in an attention task in the critical immediate post-saccadic period (0 to 100 ms following saccade offset).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the experimental approach, supported by the data collected.

claim: Performance fully recovers soon after the end of the saccade, indicating that the correct stimulus is attended to during the immediate post-saccadic period when visual sensitivity is known to be highest.
source: Our data show that performance fully recovers soon after the end of the saccade, indicating that the correct stimulus is attended to during this immediate post-sacadic period when visual sensitivity is known to be highest (Ibbotson and Krekelberg, 2011).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data, supported by citation to previous research on visual sensitivity.

claim: The retinotopic attentional shift does not impose an additional temporal cost on the resumption of visual function after a saccade.
source: The rapid time-course of recovery resembles the time-course previously shown for the recovery of visual function from saccadic suppression, suggesting that the retinotopic attentional shift does not impose an additional temporal cost on the resumption of visual function after a saccade.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with previous research on saccadic suppression recovery.

claim: Under the task conditions, subjects very rarely confuse a distractor stimulus for the target.
source: Further, our data indicate that under our task conditions, subjects very rarely confuse a distractor stimulus for the target.
evidence: This is supported by the low false-positive rates in the experimental data.

claim: Spatial attention and saccadic execution co-ordinate well to ensure that relevant objects are attentionally enhanced soon after the beginning of each eye fixation.
source: Spatial attention and saccadic execution thus appear to co-ordinate well to ensure that relevant objects are attentionally enhanced soon after the beginning of each eye fixation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the rapid recovery of performance and low false-positive rates.

claim: 10 subjects (4 males, 6 females, ages 21–30 years) participated in the study.
source: 10 subjects (4 males, 6 females, ages 21–30 years) participated in the study, including two of the authors (MK and TY).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: 8 subjects participated in Experiment 1.
source: 8, 5 and 4 subjects participated in Experiments 1, 2 and 3 respectively
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: 5 subjects participated in Experiment 2.
source: 8, 5 and 4 subjects participated in Experiments 1, 2 and 3 respectively
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: 4 subjects participated in Experiment 3.
source: 8, 5 and 4 subjects participated in Experiments 1, 2 and 3 respectively
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The median reaction-time was 324 ms.
source: The median reaction-time was 324 ms.
evidence: This is measured data from the experiment.

claim: A target RDP change occurred on about 90% of the trials.
source: A target RDP change occurred on about 90% of the trials and between 118 to 1882 ms after RDP onset; the remaining trials were catch trials and no change occurred.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: A distractor change occurred before the target change on about 39% of trials.
source: A distractor change occurred before the target change on about 39% of trials, over a similar range of times but at least 400 ms before the target change: the subject had to ignore these changes.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The fixation point jumped to a new location 7° horizontally to the right of the fixation point 1235 ms after the fixation point appeared.
source: For the saccade task, the fixation point jumped to a new location 7° horizontally to the right of the fixation point 1235 ms after the fixation point appeared.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The recovery time-course after the saccade did not seem to depend on saccade latency.
source: The recovery time-course after the saccade also did not seem to depend on saccade latency (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Very similar performance was observed when trials were grouped based on saccade latency into three groups: putative predictive saccades (latencies from 0 to 75 ms), express saccades (latencies from 75 to 125 ms) and regular-latency saccades (latencies from 125 to 250 ms).
source: Very similar performance was observed when we grouped trials based on saccade latency into three groups: putative predictive saccades (latencies from 0 to 75 ms), express saccades (latencies from 75 to 125 ms) and regular-latency saccades (latencies from 125 to 250 ms).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data analysis.

claim: Peri-saccadic attentional shifts proceed with a similar time-course for predictive, express, and regular-latency saccades.
source: This indicates that though various differences between these different kinds of saccades have been noted and these different kinds of saccades have been speculated to arise via different neural pathways (Bronstein and Kennard, 1987; Chen et al., 2013; Cotti et al., 2009; Deubel, 1995; Gaymard et al., 1998; Pierrot-Deseilligny et al., 2002; Shelhamer and Joiner, 2003), peri-saccadic attentional shifts seem to proceed with a similar time-course in each case.
evidence: This is an inference from the data showing similar recovery times across different saccade latencies, with citations to previous research on saccade types.

claim: Early responses before the target-change were extremely rare, constituting only 1.2, 1 and 0.7% of trials in Experiments 1, 2 and 3 respectively.
source: Early responses before the target-change were extremely rare: early responses constituted only 1.2, 1 and 0.7% of trials in Experiments 1, 2 and 3 respectively, even when counting all early responses that were potentially responses to the distractor change in this number.
evidence: This is measured data from the experiments.

claim: In Experiment 1, there were at least 48 trials in each 10 ms time-bin from 0 to 40 ms.
source: For Experiment 1 (Figure 2A), there were at least 48 trials in each 10 ms time-bin from 0 to 40 ms.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis.

claim: The study was performed in accordance with institutional guidelines for experiments with humans, adhered to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Georg-Elias-Müller-Institute of Psychology, University of Göttingen.
source: The study was performed in accordance with institutional guidelines for experiments with humans, adhered to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Georg-Elias-Müller-Institute of Psychology, University of Göttingen.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.
